stem: A 40-person partner team wants to adopt an engineering team's Claude Code setup for their own repository, and asks how to receive it so they can become productive without repeated hand-holding. What should the originating team provide?

opts.t: A personal override skill of the same name, added to that one engineer's own configuration, leaving the team's version untouched.
Committed, version-controlled configuration, skills, and commands, together with a guided onboarding path to follow.
A recorded walkthrough of the current setup, so the partner team can watch it at their own pace.
A shared chat channel where the partner team can ask questions about the setup as they encounter them.

whyRight: The partner team needs an artifact that survives the handoff and reaches every member regardless of who attended a walkthrough or asked a question, so a version-controlled configuration with a guided onboarding path is the only option that is actually inherited rather than person-dependent.

whyWrong.A: This fits one engineer's personal variant, not a whole team's adoption; the request is for every partner-team member to receive the setup, not for one person's individual override.
whyWrong.C: A walkthrough is durable and frozen — it teaches the setup as it exists today with full confidence on the day the setup changes and the recording does not.
whyWrong.D: A chat channel is reactive support, not an inherited artifact; it depends on someone answering each time and reaches only whoever happens to ask.

t1Clause: A 40-person partner team wants to adopt an engineering team's Claude Code setup for their own repository

stem: A weekly code-quality analysis spanning 200 repositories at a mid-size engineering org carries no fixed deadline, but each run must dynamically fetch and inspect additional related files mid-analysis before it can reach a conclusion. Which execution mode satisfies this requirement?

opts.t: Batch API, accepting the request queue because the flexible deadline yields the standard fifty-percent cost saving.
Structured JSON output enforced by a schema, so every fetched file is captured in one parseable record.
Batch API for the main pass, followed by a separate synchronous call to fetch any files it could not retrieve.
Synchronous execution, since the run must invoke tools mid-analysis before it can conclude.

whyRight: Synchronous execution is required because the analysis must call tools mid-run to fetch and inspect additional files before concluding; the Batch API cannot execute a tool mid-request and return the result, so no deadline flexibility changes which mode the mid-analysis fetch requires.

whyWrong.A: No fixed deadline suggests Batch's cost saving, but the stem already states the run must fetch files mid-analysis, a capability Batch structurally lacks regardless of the deadline.
whyWrong.B: Structured, schema-enforced output solves how findings are parsed downstream, a different question from whether the run can execute tools mid-analysis, which this option never addresses.
whyWrong.C: A follow-up synchronous call reconstructs, after the fact, exactly what running the entire analysis synchronously from the start would have done in one step.

t1Clause: each run must dynamically fetch and inspect additional related files mid-analysis before it can reach a conclusion

stem: An agent-driven pipeline at a 500-engineer, regulated financial-services firm must have a specific tool call stopped before it ever executes, with no exceptions regardless of prompt wording. Select two mechanisms that stop the call before execution.

opts.t: A hook that logs every invocation of that tool call for later audit review.
An allow rule enumerating every other tool the agent is permitted to use, leaving this one out.
A PreToolUse hook configured to block that specific tool call.
A deny rule in the permissions settings that matches that tool call.

whyRight: Both act before the call executes: a PreToolUse hook blocks it directly, and a deny permission rule is enforced by Claude Code outside the model's discretion. Either independently satisfies 'stopped before it executes, no exceptions'; a log recorded afterward or an incomplete allow-list does not.

whyWrong.A: This creates an audit trail but does not stop the call; the decision table's own contrast is explicit — both preventive mechanisms act before execution, a log acts after.
whyWrong.B: An allow-list narrows the default path but does not stop a matching call the way an explicit deny does, and it breaks any legitimate command nobody enumerated.

t1Clause: must have a specific tool call stopped before it ever executes, with no exceptions regardless of prompt wording

stem: A code-review check runs on every pull request at a 90-person org and must complete before the request can merge; a developer waits on the result before continuing other work. Which execution mode should the check use?

opts.t: Synchronous execution, so the result returns within the same request the developer is waiting on.
Batch API, deferring the check since batching costs fifty percent less than running it live.
Batch API, but poll for completion every few minutes so the developer learns as soon as it is ready.
Structured JSON output enforced by a schema, so the pipeline can parse results without a human reading them.

whyRight: The check gates the merge and a developer is actively waiting on its result, matching the row for a blocking pre-merge check: synchronous execution, because a developer is waiting on it. Nothing about cost or output format changes whether the result must return within this request.

whyWrong.B: The 'no fixed deadline' framing does not apply here — the stem already states a developer is waiting on the result before continuing, which Batch's unbounded up-to-24-hour window cannot satisfy.
whyWrong.C: Polling notifies the developer sooner but does not change Batch's lack of a latency SLA; the merge still waits on a window that can run up to 24 hours.
whyWrong.D: Nothing in the requirement asks for automated downstream parsing; the check only needs to finish before merge while a developer reads the result directly.

t1Clause: must complete before the request can merge; a developer waits on the result before continuing other work
